rows.summary: Ultra-premium global school in Chelsea; ages 1–18, bespoke curriculum, Mandarin and Spanish tracks.
rows.body: Avenues: The World School is located at 259 10th Avenue, New York, NY 10001 (Chelsea, Manhattan). Founded in 2012, it is a for-profit global school network offering a distinctive bespoke curriculum integrating Mandarin Chinese and Spanish language instruction throughout all grades. The school serves ages 1 through 18 and is known for exceptional facilities, small class sizes, and a global learning philosophy. Avenues is one of the most expensive private schools in the US — annual tuition is approximately $75,300 (2024–25 figures, full-day). Financial aid is available from kindergarten onward. The school has campuses in other world cities, appealing to internationally mobile families. Ages 1–18.

rows.title: Anglo-American International School, New York
rows.summary: Small independent international school on the Upper West Side; blending American and British educational approaches.
rows.body: The Anglo-American International School is located at 291 Central Park West / 18 West 89th Street, New York, NY 10024 (Upper West Side). It is a small, independent co-educational school blending American and British educational traditions in an international context. The school caters to a global student body and emphasises personalised education in a nurturing environment. Being a small school, it offers intimate class sizes and strong teacher-student relationships. It is a nonprofit organisation serving grades 11–12 among its upper-school provisions and welcomes expatriate families and internationally mobile students. The school is suitable for families seeking a more personalised alternative to larger international schools.

rows.title: International School of Brooklyn (ISB)
rows.summary: French-English and Spanish-English bilingual IB school in Carroll Gardens; ages 3–14 (PreK–Grade 8).
rows.body: The International School of Brooklyn is located at 477 Court Street (Main Campus) and 192 Luquer Street, Brooklyn, NY 11231 (Carroll Gardens). ISB offers French-English and Spanish-English bilingual programs for students from age 3 through Grade 8 (ages 3–14). It is an IB World School offering the Primary Years Programme. The school has approximately 388 students and is known for its multicultural community and genuine bilingual education. Annual tuition ranges from approximately $36,269 to $52,537 depending on grade level (2024–25). ISB granted over $2.9 million in tuition assistance. Situated in a family-friendly Brooklyn neighbourhood within walking distance of the F/G subway trains.

rows.title: British International School of New York (BIS-NY)
rows.summary: British-curriculum international school in Kips Bay (Waterside Plaza); ages 2–18, National Curriculum of England plus A-levels.
rows.body: The British International School of New York is located at 20 Waterside Plaza (23rd Street & East River), New York, NY 10010 (Kips Bay / Midtown East waterfront). BIS-NY follows the National Curriculum of England and offers GCSEs and A-Levels alongside the school's holistic programme. The school serves ages 2–18 (Nursery 2s through Year 13 / Grade 12). It is a popular choice for British expat families and families familiar with the English educational system. Annual tuition ranges from approximately $45,600 (Nursery) to $66,700–$67,800 (Years 1–13) for 2024–25. BIS-NY is a Nord Anglia Education school offering enrichment programmes developed with Juilliard, MIT, and UNICEF. The Waterside Plaza campus has extensive facilities including a sports hall and swimming pool.

rows.title: Nord Anglia International School New York (NAISNY)
rows.summary: British-inspired international school in Lower Manhattan; ages 2–14, enrichment with Juilliard and MIT.
rows.body: Nord Anglia International School New York (NAISNY) is located at 44 East 2nd Street, New York, NY 10003 (NoHo / Lower Manhattan). It serves students aged 2 to 14 (Nursery through Year 9), following a British-inspired international curriculum enriched through Nord Anglia's global partnerships with Juilliard School of Music, MIT, and UNICEF. Approximately 200 students attend across early years and primary/middle school phases. Annual tuition ranges from approximately $36,800 (Nursery) to $57,800 (upper years, 2024–25). The school's small size allows for personalised attention. Families seeking continuation for older students typically transition to BIS-NY or other schools at age 14+.

rows.title: Chelsea / South Kensington (SW3/SW7)
rows.summary: Ultra-premium London neighbourhood; embassies, Lycée Français, French community, world-class museums.
rows.body: Chelsea and South Kensington form one of London's most prestigious and internationally recognised residential corridors. South Kensington (SW7) is home to the Lycée Français Charles de Gaulle (35 Cromwell Road), the Victoria and Albert Museum, Natural History Museum, and Science Museum — making it a cultural hub especially popular with French, Italian, and Spanish diplomatic families. Chelsea (SW3) is renowned for the King's Road, the Chelsea Physic Garden, and a dense concentration of embassies. The area attracts diplomats, corporate executives, and wealthy international families. Excellent transport: District and Circle lines (South Kensington, Sloane Square stations). Properties range from Edwardian flats to stucco-fronted Georgian townhouses.
rows.district: Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea — SW3/SW7

rows.title: Notting Hill / Holland Park (W11/W14)
rows.summary: Leafy, premium west London neighbourhood; arts community, Portobello Road, family-friendly garden squares.
rows.body: Notting Hill (W11) and Holland Park (W14) are among west London's most desirable residential addresses, combining leafy streets, gracious stucco townhouses, and a vibrant arts and creative community. Holland Park itself — one of London's finest Royal Parks — forms the centrepiece, with peacocks, the Kyoto Japanese Garden, and excellent sports facilities. Notting Hill is famous for its Portobello Road Market, independent boutiques, and the Notting Hill Carnival. The area has long attracted international artists, filmmakers, media professionals, and families. Excellent transit: Central line (Holland Park, Notting Hill Gate stations), Circle/District lines. The neighbourhood is within easy reach of multiple international schools in the Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea.
rows.district: Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea / London Borough of Hammersmith and Fulham — W11/W14

rows.title: Fulham / Parsons Green (SW6)
rows.summary: Popular expat family neighbourhood in south-west London; school-run culture, mid-premium rents, good community feel.
rows.body: Fulham and Parsons Green (SW6) are the quintessential expat family neighbourhoods of London, with a dense concentration of international families — particularly Australian, South African, American, and French expats. The area has an excellent 'school-run culture' with numerous good primary schools and proximity to several international schools. Parsons Green village has a strong café, restaurant, and pub scene. The Hurlingham Club (private sports and social club) is located here. Bishop's Park and the Thames Path provide ample outdoor space. Rents are mid-to-upper range relative to London overall, but significantly below Chelsea or Kensington. Transit: District line (Parsons Green, Fulham Broadway). The area is walkable and cycle-friendly.
rows.district: London Borough of Hammersmith and Fulham — SW6

rows.title: Hampstead / Highgate (NW3/N6)
rows.summary: Village-feel north London neighbourhood; premium, writers and academics, Hampstead Heath, excellent schools.
rows.body: Hampstead (NW3) and Highgate (N6) sit on the northern heights of London overlooking the city from above Hampstead Heath — 790 acres of ancient woodland, open grassland, and bathing ponds. The area has historically attracted writers, academics, artists, and intellectuals (Keats, Karl Marx, and Sigmund Freud all lived here). Both neighbourhoods have a genuine village high street feel, with independent shops, bookshops, and restaurants. Southbank International School (Hampstead Campus) serves ages 2–11 at its NW3 location. Multiple excellent state and independent schools nearby. Transit: Northern line (Hampstead, Highgate, Golders Green stations). Premium property prices reflect the lifestyle quality and green space access.
rows.district: London Borough of Camden / Haringey — NW3/N6

rows.title: Richmond / Kew (SW/Surrey Border)
rows.summary: Riverside suburban neighbourhood with excellent schools; the German School London is in Richmond, ideal for families.
rows.body: Richmond upon Thames is consistently ranked among the UK's best places to live, combining riverside beauty, outstanding schools (both state and independent), and a semi-rural feel with easy central London access. Richmond Park — 2,500 acres of Royal Deer Park — is the largest Royal Park in London. Kew Gardens (Royal Botanic Gardens) is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The German School London (Deutsche Schule London) is located at Douglas House, Petersham Road, Richmond TW10 — making this the natural home for German expatriate families. The International School of London (ISL) is in nearby Chiswick (W3). Transit: District line, London Overground, South Western Railway. Property is predominantly houses and garden flats.
rows.district: London Borough of Richmond upon Thames — TW9/TW10

rows.title: Wimbledon (SW19)
rows.summary: Prestigious south-west London neighbourhood; quiet, family-friendly, excellent schools, world-famous tennis venue.
rows.body: Wimbledon (SW19) is one of South West London's most coveted residential neighbourhoods, best known for hosting the annual Wimbledon Tennis Championships but equally esteemed for its outstanding state and independent schools, village high street atmosphere, and generous green spaces including Wimbledon Common (1,100 acres). Wimbledon Village (the higher-elevation part around the All England Club) offers premium boutiques and restaurants. The neighbourhood attracts international families — particularly those from the Americas and Scandinavia — drawn by its school options and quality of life. Transit: District line, South Western Railway (fast trains to Waterloo, 20 minutes). Easy access to the A3 for those driving to the City or Surrey suburbs.

rows.title: Islington / Angel (N1)
rows.summary: Trendy, central north London neighbourhood; creative professionals, young families, Georgian townhouses, excellent transit.
rows.body: Islington (N1) and its southern gateway 'Angel' have transformed from working-class roots into one of London's most fashionable and politically active boroughs. The area is particularly popular with media professionals, lawyers, tech workers, and internationally-minded young families attracted by central location, good transport, vibrant restaurant and pub culture along Upper Street, and attractive Georgian and Victorian terraced housing stock. The area has seen significant gentrification and now offers premium living at slightly lower prices than Kensington/Chelsea equivalents. Transit: Victoria and Piccadilly lines (Highbury & Islington, Angel, King's Cross); Overground. Multiple good local schools and proximity to central London institutions.

rows.title: Shoreditch / Hackney (E1/E8)
rows.summary: Tech and creative hub in east London; young international expats, mid-range rents, vibrant arts and dining scene.
rows.body: Shoreditch (E1) and Hackney (E8) form London's foremost technology and creative hub, home to the 'Silicon Roundabout' at Old Street and a dense cluster of tech start-ups, digital agencies, design studios, and creative businesses. The area attracts younger international expats from the US, Australia, France, Germany, and across Europe working in tech, media, and the creative industries. Brick Lane offers a vibrant food, arts, and vintage shopping scene. Broadway Market in Hackney is a celebrated independent food market. Rents are mid-range compared to west London. Transit: Overground, Hammersmith & City/Metropolitan lines (Shoreditch/Bethnal Green), Elizabeth line (Liverpool Street, Whitechapel). The area is cycle-friendly with strong cycling infrastructure.
rows.district: London Borough of Hackney / Tower Hamlets — E1/E8

rows.title: Canary Wharf / Isle of Dogs (E14)
rows.summary: London's financial district 2.0; corporate expats in finance, waterfront towers, excellent Crossrail connectivity.
rows.body: Canary Wharf and the Isle of Dogs (E14) form London's second financial centre, housing the headquarters of major global banks, law firms, and financial institutions. The area is dominated by high-rise residential and commercial towers with extensive waterfront promenades along the West India Docks and Thames. Popular with corporate expats in banking, finance, insurance, and professional services. The Crossrail (Elizabeth line) station at Canary Wharf provides fast connections — 7 minutes to Liverpool Street, 14 minutes to Bond Street, 13 minutes to Heathrow (direct). Also served by the DLR and Jubilee line. Limited green space compared to west/south-west London but good indoor leisure facilities and the O2 Arena nearby in Greenwich. Rents are mid-to-premium.
rows.district: London Borough of Tower Hamlets — E14

rows.title: Greenwich (SE10)
rows.summary: Historic riverside neighbourhood; UNESCO World Heritage Site, family-friendly, good value vs central London.
rows.body: Greenwich (SE10) offers a compelling mix of maritime history, parkland, and genuine family-friendliness at prices significantly below comparable central or west London neighbourhoods. Greenwich Park (Royal Park, 183 acres) sits above the town, with the Royal Observatory at its summit. The historic town centre features the Cutty Sark clipper ship, the National Maritime Museum, the Old Royal Naval College (a UNESCO World Heritage Site), and a popular Sunday market. The Meridian Line passes through the borough. Transit: DLR (Cutty Sark, Greenwich), Elizabeth line (Woolwich, nearby), Thames Clipper ferry services to central London. Nord Anglia International School (Bethnal Green) is accessible via the DLR/Overground. Growing expat community particularly from France, Germany, and the Americas.

rows.title: Battersea / Clapham (SW8/SW4)
rows.summary: Popular young family neighbourhood; South Bank proximity, Battersea Power Station development, thriving expat community.
rows.body: Battersea (SW8) and Clapham (SW4) are two of South London's most popular neighbourhoods for young professional expat families. Battersea Power Station has been redeveloped into a major mixed-use destination with luxury apartments, retail, restaurants, and a new Northern line extension. Battersea Park (200 acres, with a zoo and riverside walk) is a major asset. Clapham Common is a beloved community space used year-round. Clapham has a strong Australian, South African, and international expat community. Rents are more accessible than equivalent properties in west London. Transit: Northern line (Clapham Common, Clapham South, Battersea Power Station — new station opened 2021). Excellent cycling routes to the City and West End.
rows.district: London Borough of Wandsworth / Lambeth — SW8/SW4

rows.title: St John's Wood (NW8)
rows.summary: Premium north-west London neighbourhood; home to the American School in London, embassies, Regent's Park proximity.
rows.body: St John's Wood (NW8) is one of London's premier residential neighbourhoods and the most internationally-oriented outside of the traditional embassy belt. It is home to the American School in London (ASL), which anchors a substantial American expat community in the surrounding streets. Lord's Cricket Ground is nearby, as is Regent's Park (one of London's finest Royal Parks). The neighbourhood features wide, tree-lined streets, detached and semi-detached Victorian villas, and a village-like high street. Heavily international — American, French, Israeli, Indian, and Middle Eastern families are particularly well represented. Transit: Jubilee line (St John's Wood station, direct to Canary Wharf in 12 minutes, Bond Street in 4 minutes). Premium property prices reflect the international demand.

rows.title: Kensington / Hyde Park (W8)
rows.summary: Ultra-premium west London enclave; embassies, Kensington Palace, Southbank International School (Kensington campus).
rows.body: Kensington (W8) and the Hyde Park area represent London's most prestigious and expensive residential addresses, comparable globally to Manhattan's Upper East Side or Paris's 16th arrondissement. Kensington Palace, the official residence of multiple members of the Royal Family, is located here. The neighbourhood is home to numerous national embassies and high commissions, making it the epicentre of London's diplomatic community. Kensington High Street offers upscale retail. The Southbank International School's Kensington campus (for ages 2–11) is located at 37 Chepstow Villas, W11 — adjacent to the W8 area. Hyde Park (350 acres) provides exceptional green space and recreational facilities. Transit: District and Circle lines (High Street Kensington, Kensington Olympia).
rows.district: Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea — W8

rows.title: Stratford / Westfield (E15)
rows.summary: East London Olympic legacy zone; budget-friendly, excellent transport hub, regenerated with shopping and cultural venues.
rows.body: Stratford (E15) was transformed by the 2012 London Olympics into one of east London's most ambitious regeneration zones. The Olympic Park (now the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park) provides 560 acres of parkland, world-class sports venues, the London Aquatics Centre, Velodrome, the London Stadium, and the Here East innovation campus. Westfield Stratford City — Europe's largest urban shopping centre — is adjacent. New residential developments provide modern apartments at below-average London prices. Increasingly attractive to young international professionals working in tech and start-ups at Here East or commuting to the City/Canary Wharf. Transit: Elizabeth line, Jubilee line, DLR, c2c rail, Overground — one of London's best-connected stations. Budget-friendly for London.

rows.title: American School in London (ASL)
rows.summary: Leading American PreK–12 day school in St John's Wood NW8; US curriculum, college-preparatory, ages 4–18.
rows.body: The American School in London is located at 1 Waverley Place, London NW8 0NP (St John's Wood). Founded in 1951, it is an independent, college-preparatory, PreK–12 day school providing an American education to an international community of approximately 1,350 students from over 60 countries. ASL offers the US college-preparatory curriculum and is accredited by the New England Association of Schools and Colleges (NEASC). It is among the UK's most expensive day schools. Annual tuition for 2025–26 (including VAT) is £40,188 (Lower School), £44,616 (Middle School), and £46,428 (High School). Grades 9–12 tuition reaches £49,932 per year. Ages 4–18. The school is the anchor of the large American expat community in St John's Wood.
rows.district: City of Westminster — St John's Wood, NW8

rows.title: Lycée Français Charles de Gaulle
rows.summary: French government school in South Kensington; ages 3–18, French Ministry curriculum, highly subsidised fees for French nationals.
rows.body: The Lycée Français Charles de Gaulle is located at 35 Cromwell Road, London SW7 2DG (South Kensington). It is managed by the AEFE (Agence pour l'Enseignement Français à l'Étranger) and serves as France's flagship school in the United Kingdom. With approximately 3,300 students, it is one of the largest French schools outside France. The school follows the French Ministry of Education curriculum from Maternelle (age 3) through Terminale (age 18/19), preparing students for the French Baccalaureate. Fees are heavily subsidised for French nationals (approximately £10,297–£12,557/year for primary, £13,220–£21,542/year for secondary including VAT for 2026–27). Non-French nationals pay higher fees. Ages 3–18.
rows.district: Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea — South Kensington, SW7
rows.price_range_text: £10,297–£21,542/year (2025–26, incl. VAT; French nationals eligible for subsidised rates)

rows.title: German School London (Deutsche Schule London)
rows.summary: German-curriculum international school in Richmond, SW London; ages 3–18, German Abitur, bilingual education.
rows.body: The German School London (Deutsche Schule London) is located at Douglas House, Petersham Road, Petersham, Richmond, Surrey TW10 7AH. It is an independent school set in a spacious, green site between Richmond Park and the Thames. The school offers a German-curriculum education from Kindergarten (age 3) through Year 12/Abitur (age 18/19) and is popular with German corporate expat families and those from German-speaking countries (Austria, Switzerland). Approximately 600–700 students attend. Annual tuition is approximately £10,920–£13,280/year (incl. VAT, 2024–25 figures), making it one of London's most affordable international schools. Ages 3–18/19. The school is officially recognised by the German state of Berlin.
rows.district: London Borough of Richmond upon Thames — Petersham/Richmond, TW10

rows.title: Nord Anglia International School London (NAISL)
rows.summary: IB international school in Bethnal Green / Tower Hamlets; ages 2–18, enrichment via Juilliard and MIT partnerships.
rows.body: Nord Anglia International School London is located in the Bethnal Green area of east London (Tower Hamlets, E2). As part of the Nord Anglia Education global network, the school follows an IB-aligned international curriculum enriched through unique partnerships with Juilliard School of Music, MIT, and UNICEF. The school serves approximately 650 students aged 2 to 18 across early years, primary, and secondary phases. Annual tuition ranges from approximately £20,877 to £48,099 (2024–25). The school benefits from modern, purpose-built facilities and a diverse international student body representing 60+ nationalities. IB Diploma Programme offered in Years 12–13. Well-connected via the Overground and Elizabeth line (Bethnal Green, Whitechapel).
rows.district: London Borough of Tower Hamlets — Bethnal Green, E2

rows.title: ACS International Schools (Cobham / Egham)
rows.summary: American-curriculum international schools in Surrey suburbs; IB and US curriculum, ages 2–18, day and boarding.
rows.body: ACS International Schools operates two campuses accessible from London: ACS Cobham (Portsmouth Road, Cobham, Surrey KT11) and ACS Egham (London Road, Egham, Surrey TW20 0HS). Both campuses offer an American-influenced international education using IB programmes (Cobham was the first school in the UK to offer all four IB programmes). ACS Cobham caters to ages 2–18 (day pupils); ACS Egham ages 3–18 (day and boarding). Day tuition at Cobham: approximately £35,400–£39,720/year for secondary (Grades 7–11). Day tuition at Egham: approximately £15,540–£37,440/year. Both campuses are popular with US corporate expat families and international families in the Surrey/south-west London commuter belt. Heathrow proximity is a draw for families with frequent international travel.

rows.title: International School of London (ISL)
rows.summary: IB World School in Chiswick, west London; ages 3–18, full IB continuum, multilingual community.
rows.body: The International School of London is located at 139 Gunnersbury Avenue, London W3 8LG (Chiswick, west London). ISL offers the full International Baccalaureate continuum from Early Childhood (age 3) through the IB Diploma Programme (ages 17–18) to approximately 395 students from over 60 countries. The school emphasises multilingualism — students maintain their mother tongue alongside English and an additional language. Annual tuition for 2026–27 is approximately £24,630 (Early Childhood Year 1, age 3) to £39,940 (IB Diploma years). The school is co-educational and non-selective. Located near the A4/M4 corridor for families commuting from west London or Heathrow vicinity. Ages 3–18.
rows.district: London Borough of Hounslow — Chiswick, W3/W5

rows.title: Southbank International School
rows.summary: Multi-campus IB World School; Hampstead (ages 2–11), Westminster and Kensington (ages 11–18); trilingual approach.
rows.body: Southbank International School operates across three London campuses: Hampstead Campus (NW3, ages 2–11), Westminster Campus (377–381 Euston Road, NW1, ages 11–18), and Kensington Campus (W11, ages 2–11). Together they serve approximately 900 students aged 2–18 from over 50 countries. The school offers the full IB continuum (PYP, MYP, DP, CP). Annual tuition ranges from approximately £20,877 to £48,099 depending on campus and year group (2024–25). The school has a strong reputation for global-mindedness and language education. The Westminster campus occupies a purpose-built building near King's Cross. Ages 2–18 across all campuses. Southbank is particularly popular with European diplomatic and corporate expat families.
rows.district: London Borough of Camden — Hampstead (NW3) / Westminster / Kensington

rows.title: The King Alfred School (KAS)
rows.summary: Progressive co-educational independent day school in Golders Green NW11; ages 4–18, international student body, child-centred philosophy.
rows.body: The King Alfred School is located at 149 North End Road, Golders Green, London NW11 7HY. It is one of the UK's oldest and most distinguished progressive independent schools, founded in 1898 on child-centred principles. KAS is co-educational, non-selective, and prides itself on a nurturing, informal atmosphere that respects each child's individuality. The school serves approximately 600 students aged 4–18 across lower school (Reception through Year 6) and upper school (Years 7–13). Annual fees range from approximately £24,531 to £30,156 (per year; including VAT from 2025). The school attracts a significant number of international families — particularly from continental Europe, the US, and Israel — drawn to its non-conformist reputation. Ages 4–18.
rows.district: London Borough of Barnet — Golders Green, NW11

rows.title: Oud-Zuid (Old South)
rows.summary: Upmarket residential; Vondelpark, museums, expat families.
rows.body: Amsterdam's Oud-Zuid district is home to the Vondelpark, Rijksmuseum, and Concertgebouw. The most popular area for corporate expats. Tree-lined streets with period townhouses and modern apartments. Strong English-speaking community. Very family-friendly. Amsterdam International Community School is nearby. Rental prices are the highest in Amsterdam. Well-served by tram routes 2, 3, 5.

rows.title: De Pijp
rows.summary: Multicultural, bohemian neighbourhood; Albert Cuyp market, cafés, mid-range rents.
rows.body: De Pijp is Amsterdam's most cosmopolitan and vibrant neighbourhood, home to the famous Albert Cuyp street market. The area is beloved by young professionals, artists, and international families seeking a lively community with excellent restaurants, brown cafés, and independent boutiques. Good tram connections to the centre. Mid-range rents make it attractive for expats not on corporate housing packages. Close to De Pijp metro station on the North-South line.

rows.title: Jordaan
rows.summary: Historic canal district; charming, restaurants, popular with young professionals and expats.
rows.body: The Jordaan is one of Amsterdam's most charming neighbourhoods, known for its 17th-century canal houses, narrow streets, art galleries, boutique shops, and excellent restaurants. Highly sought after by young professionals and expats who value character and walkability. Close to the Anne Frank House and Westerkerk. Very central, with excellent cycling infrastructure. Rents are high due to strong demand and limited supply of family-sized properties.

rows.title: Centrum / Canal Ring
rows.summary: Historic centre; UNESCO-listed canals, tourist-heavy, limited family housing, expensive.
rows.body: Amsterdam Centrum and the Canal Ring (Grachtengordeel) form the UNESCO-listed historic heart of the city. Home to world-class museums, the Dam Square, and the Red Light District. The area is very popular with tourists and short-term renters, making long-term family housing scarce and expensive. Limited green space. Excellent public transport connections to all parts of the city. Best suited for singles or couples rather than families.

rows.title: Oud-West
rows.summary: Cosy residential neighbourhood; cafés, local shops, younger professionals, mid-range.
rows.body: Oud-West sits just west of the Centrum and has a cosy, neighbourhood feel with many local cafés, restaurants, and independent shops. Popular with younger professionals and couples. The Ten Katemarkt is a favourite local market. Good cycling infrastructure and tram connections. Quieter than De Pijp but equally well-connected. Rents are mid-range for Amsterdam standards.

rows.title: Watergraafsmeer / Plantage
rows.summary: Quieter, more residential east Amsterdam; parks, zoo, mid-range rents.
rows.body: Watergraafsmeer and Plantage are quieter, predominantly residential neighbourhoods east of the Centrum. Plantage is home to the Artis Royal Zoo, the Hortus Botanicus botanical garden, and the Dutch Resistance Museum. Watergraafsmeer offers more space for the same price compared to central Amsterdam. The British School of Amsterdam (BSN) is located here. Good tram and metro connections.

rows.title: Amsterdam Noord
rows.summary: Up-and-coming creative district north of the IJ river; lower rents, vibrant arts scene.
rows.body: Amsterdam Noord has transformed from an industrial area to a thriving creative hub. Free ferry services across the IJ river connect it to Centraal Station in minutes. Home to the EYE Film Museum, A'DAM Tower, and the NDSM wharf, a creative hotspot. Rents are significantly lower than in the centre. Increasingly popular with younger expats and creatives. Growing number of restaurants and cultural venues.

rows.title: Badhoevedorp / Amstelveen
rows.summary: Suburban south near Schiphol; large expat community, many international schools, garden houses.
rows.body: Amstelveen and neighbouring Badhoevedorp are the most popular suburban areas for corporate expats relocating to the Amsterdam region. Amstelveen is home to significant Japanese, South Korean, and US communities, and hosts the International School of Amsterdam (ISA) and Amity International School Amsterdam. Properties are larger and often include gardens. Quick access to Schiphol Airport via the A9 motorway. More suburban in character but with good local amenities.

rows.title: Buitenveldert / Zuid
rows.summary: Residential south Amsterdam; RAI convention centre, international schools, good transport.
rows.body: Buitenveldert is a quiet, residential neighbourhood in Amsterdam's southern district, popular with expat families. The Amsterdam International Community School (AICS) has campuses in this area. Close to the RAI convention centre and Amsterdam ArenA. Good metro connections to Schiphol and the city centre. Mix of apartments and terraced houses. Well-suited for families who want to stay within Amsterdam city limits but in a calmer environment.

rows.title: IJburg
rows.summary: Modern waterfront island neighbourhood; family-friendly, newer housing, commuter community.
rows.body: IJburg is a relatively new neighbourhood built on artificial islands in the IJmeer lake east of Amsterdam. Known for its modern architecture, waterfront living, and family-friendly atmosphere. Popular with young families priced out of central Amsterdam. Tram 26 connects it directly to Centraal Station in about 25 minutes. Good schools, sports facilities, and a growing number of local shops and restaurants. Sandy beaches along the waterfront in summer.

rows.title: Amsterdam International Community School (AICS)
rows.summary: All-IB international school; ages 4–18; South and South-East Amsterdam campuses.
rows.body: AICS is the first Dutch international school to offer all four IB programmes (PYP, MYP, DP, CP). Accepts students from age 4 to 18. Operates two permanent campuses in Amsterdam South (Buitenveldert) and South-East. Annual tuition approximately €6,000–€18,000 depending on year group and programme (subsidised through Dutch government guidelines for international schools). Strong English-speaking community; serves expat families across multiple nationalities.

rows.title: The British School of Amsterdam (BSN)
rows.summary: Independent British curriculum day school; ages 3–18; Watergraafsmeer.
rows.body: Located at Havenstraat 6, 1075 PR Amsterdam (Watergraafsmeer area). Co-educational, non-profit independent school following the National Curriculum for England through to GCSEs and A-Levels. Ages 3–18 (Nursery through Year 13). Annual tuition 2025–26: Nursery from €9,375; Reception/Year 1 €19,884; Junior School Years 2–6 €20,277; Senior School Years 7–13 €21,528. Accredited by the British Schools Overseas (BSO) inspectorate.

rows.title: International School of Amsterdam (ISA)
rows.summary: Pioneer IB World School; ages 2–18; full IB continuum; Amstelveen.
rows.body: Located at Sportlaan 45, 1185 TB Amstelveen. ISA was the first school in the world to offer a complete IB curriculum from Pre-School to Grade 12. Offers IB Early Years (ages 2–3), IB Primary Years (ages 3–12), IB Middle Years (ages 12–16) and IB Diploma (ages 16–18). Close to 1,300 students representing over 60 nationalities. Annual tuition 2023–24 ranged from €19,900 (Nursery) to €28,565 (Grade 12), plus a capital fee of €3,075.

rows.title: Amity International School Amsterdam (AISA)
rows.summary: Not-for-profit IB World School; ages 3–18; full IB continuum; Amstelveen.
rows.body: Located at Amsterdamseweg 204, 1182 HL Amstelveen. An accredited IB World School offering the full IB Continuum from Early Years through the IB Diploma Programme for ages 3–18. Annual tuition 2026–27: Early Years €20,950; Primary Years €21,785; Middle Years €23,365; Diploma Programme €26,905. Small classes, multicultural community, optional door-to-door transport. Not-for-profit; fees reinvested in education.

rows.title: Japanese School of Amsterdam (JSA)
rows.summary: Full-time Japanese national curriculum day school; ages 6–15; western Amsterdam.
rows.body: Located at Karel Klinkenbergstraat 137, 1061 AL Amsterdam. Follows the Japanese national curriculum (grades 1–9, elementary and junior high school levels). Language of instruction is Japanese; students in grades 1–5 are also required to take Dutch classes. Primarily serves the children of Japanese expatriate families temporarily based in the Netherlands. Approximately 42 students. Not open to non-Japanese students in general.
rows.price_range_text: Fees not publicly listed (Japanese government subsidised)

rows.title: Ballsbridge / Donnybrook (D4)
rows.summary: Embassy quarter; premium residential, corporate expats, top schools, leafy streets.
rows.body: Dublin 4's Ballsbridge is the most prestigious address for corporate expats in Ireland, home to embassies, the RDS (Royal Dublin Society), Aviva Stadium, and several five-star hotels. Tree-lined streets of large Victorian and Edwardian houses attract senior corporate executives and diplomats. Excellent access to the DART coastal rail line, the N11, and the city centre. Close proximity to the Dodder river greenway. Some of the highest rents in Ireland.

rows.title: Ranelagh / Rathmines (D6)
rows.summary: Vibrant, walkable village; young professionals, restaurants, cafés, mid-premium rents.
rows.body: Ranelagh and Rathmines are among Dublin's most popular addresses for young professionals and expat couples. Ranelagh village offers a superb range of independent restaurants, cafés, and boutiques within easy walking distance of each other. Sandford Park School is located in Ranelagh. The Luas Green Line tram runs directly into the city centre and onwards to Sandyford and Cherrywood. A neighbourhood with a strong community feel.

rows.title: Dundrum / Rathfarnham (D14/D16)
rows.summary: Suburban south Dublin; family-focused, top schools, Dundrum Town Centre, Luas access.
rows.body: Dundrum and Rathfarnham are highly sought-after suburban areas in south Dublin, extremely popular with expat families. Dundrum Town Centre is one of Ireland's premier shopping destinations. Excellent selection of schools including fee-paying schools and sports clubs. Served by the Luas Green Line tram. More affordable than Ballsbridge or Ranelagh while still offering a premium suburban lifestyle. Rathfarnham has access to the Dublin Mountains for outdoor activities.

rows.title: Blackrock / Dún Laoghaire (Coastal D4 / Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown)
rows.summary: DART-connected coastal villages; family-friendly, yacht clubs, scenic sea views, premium.
rows.body: Blackrock and Dún Laoghaire sit along Dublin Bay's south coast, offering a relaxed village atmosphere with seaside walks, yacht clubs, and independent cafés. The DART commuter rail line connects them to the city centre in 20–30 minutes. Popular with families and professionals who value outdoor lifestyle. Dún Laoghaire's East Pier is a beloved walk. Access to good schools including Rathdown School in nearby Glenageary. Generally premium-priced.

rows.title: Clontarf (D3)
rows.summary: Coastal north Dublin village; family-friendly, Clontarf promenade, good schools, DART access.
rows.body: Clontarf is a well-established north Dublin coastal suburb with a village feel and popular seaside promenade along Dublin Bay. Extremely family-friendly with excellent primary and secondary schools, sports clubs (GAA, rugby, cricket), and a strong community spirit. The DART connects residents to the city centre in about 15 minutes. Close to Saint Anne's Park, a large public park. Slightly more affordable than D4 equivalents south of the Liffey.

rows.title: Howth / Malahide (North Coast, D13)
rows.summary: Scenic north Dublin coastal villages; premium, commutable, sailing community, fishing harbour.
rows.body: Howth and Malahide are picturesque fishing and sailing villages on Dublin's north coast. Howth Head offers dramatic cliff walks and a busy harbour. Malahide has a charming village centre and a medieval castle. Both are served by the DART rail line, making them commutable to the city centre in 30–40 minutes. Popular with senior corporate expats and families seeking a scenic, quieter lifestyle while remaining within easy reach of Dublin Airport and the city.

rows.title: Sandyford / Leopardstown (D18)
rows.summary: South Dublin tech hub; near Google/Salesforce offices, Luas Green Line, good value.
rows.body: Sandyford is home to a major business district hosting offices of Google, Salesforce, LinkedIn, and many other multinationals. The International School of Dublin (ISD) is located here. Well served by the Luas Green Line tram. Leopardstown Racecourse is nearby. More affordable than central D4 districts while offering modern apartments and good amenities. A practical choice for expat professionals working in the south Dublin tech corridor. Access to the M50 motorway.

rows.title: Portmarnock / Sutton (D13)
rows.summary: Quiet north Dublin coastal suburbs; family-focused, golf courses, DART access.
rows.body: Portmarnock and Sutton are quiet, predominantly residential coastal communities on north Dublin's peninsula. Known for their golf courses (Portmarnock Golf Club is world-famous), clean beaches, and relaxed family-friendly atmosphere. The DART connects Sutton to the city centre. Popular with families seeking space and a quieter pace of life. Less international school infrastructure than south Dublin but within easy reach of Dublin Airport. Very safe neighbourhoods.

rows.title: Cabinteely / Killiney (D18)
rows.summary: Affluent south Dublin coastal suburb; stunning sea views, celebrity neighbourhood, premium.
rows.body: Killiney is often called the 'Irish Riviera' for its dramatic coastal scenery and clifftop sea views over Dublin Bay. An affluent, leafy suburb popular with senior executives and celebrities. Killiney Hill offers outstanding walking routes. Served by the DART. Cabinteely is a quieter adjoining suburb with good local amenities and schools. Both areas offer large detached houses in green settings. Quiet and exclusive.

rows.title: City Centre / Docklands (D1/D2)
rows.summary: Silicon Docks; Google, Facebook, LinkedIn HQs, young professionals, vibrant cultural scene.
rows.body: Dublin's City Centre and Docklands (Grand Canal Dock area) form the heart of Ireland's tech economy, hosting European HQs of Google, Meta, LinkedIn, Twitter/X, and many other multinationals. The Docklands is a modern, high-density neighbourhood with luxury apartments along the Liffey and Grand Canal. Excellent restaurants, bars, theatres, and cultural venues. Popular with young professionals and expat singles or couples without children. Good transport links including Luas, buses, and the planned MetroLink.

rows.title: St. Andrew's College Dublin
rows.summary: Fee-paying co-educational through-school offering IB; ages 4–18; Booterstown, D4.
rows.body: Located on Booterstown Avenue, Blackrock, Co. Dublin. Ireland's only school offering the International Baccalaureate Diploma Programme alongside the Irish Leaving Certificate. Co-educational, non-denominational, independent fee-paying school for ages 4–18. Approximately 1,300 students. Annual fees approximately €9,100–€12,000 per year depending on year level. Strong sports, arts, and academic programmes. Popular with expat families for its IB offering and international community.

rows.title: International School of Dublin (ISD)
rows.summary: Small co-educational IB Primary Years school; ages 3–12; Synge Street, Dublin 8.
rows.body: Located at Synge Street, Dublin 8. A culturally diverse, private, not-for-profit co-educational and non-denominational school. Offers the IB Primary Years Programme for children aged 3.5 to 12. Accepts year-round enrolments. Annual tuition approximately €11,250 per year. One of the few dedicated international schools within Dublin city itself. Popular with expat families in the tech sector who live centrally.

rows.title: Nord Anglia International School Dublin (NAIS Dublin)
rows.summary: Leading international school; ages 3–18; British and IB curriculum; Sandyford.
rows.body: Located in Sandyford, Dublin 18. Part of the global Nord Anglia Education group. Co-educational school for students aged 3 to 18, offering the British National Curriculum and IB Diploma Programme. Early Years (ages 3–6), Primary (ages 6–11), Secondary (ages 11–18). Annual fees from approximately €15,900 to €22,000+ depending on year group. Strong links with MIT, Juilliard, and UNICEF through Nord Anglia's global network.

rows.title: Sandford Park School
rows.summary: Small progressive co-educational secondary day school; ages 12–18; Ranelagh, D6.
rows.body: Located on Sandford Road, Ranelagh, Dublin 6. A small, progressive, private, non-denominational, co-educational secondary school for students aged 12 to 18. Approximately 350 students. Follows the Irish state secondary curriculum (Junior and Leaving Certificate). Annual day fees approximately €7,150. Founded in 1922, known for its strong pastoral care, small class sizes, and inclusive environment. Popular with expat families for its progressive and non-denominational ethos.

rows.title: Rathdown School
rows.summary: Day and boarding school; ages 3–18; co-educational; Upper Glenageary Road, Glenageary.
rows.body: Located on Upper Glenageary Road, Glenageary, Co. Dublin, near Dún Laoghaire. A co-educational day and boarding school for boys and girls aged 3 to 18 (pre-school through Leaving Certificate). Follows the Irish national curriculum. Approximately 450 students. Fees vary by year group; day fees from approximately €8,200 per year for secondary. Also accepts international boarding students. Well-regarded for its holistic, inclusive, and academically progressive approach.

rows.title: Minato-ku (Azabu-Juban, Hiroo, Roppongi)
rows.summary: Premier expat district; embassies, international schools, restaurants, premium rents.
rows.body: Minato-ku is the most popular ward for expatriates in Tokyo, particularly the neighbourhoods of Azabu-Juban, Hiroo, and Roppongi. Home to numerous embassies, international clubs, and a dense concentration of international schools (Nishimachi, ISSH, British School primary campus). Hiroo has a well-established expat shopping strip with international supermarkets. Roppongi offers world-class nightlife and arts venues (Mori Art Museum, National Art Center). Very expensive; rents are among the highest in Tokyo. Excellent subway access.

rows.title: Shibuya-ku
rows.summary: Trendy urban hub; iconic crossing, shopping, dining, younger expats and creatives.
rows.body: Shibuya-ku is one of Tokyo's most vibrant wards, home to the world-famous Shibuya Crossing and some of the city's best shopping, dining, and entertainment. Neighbourhoods like Daikanyama, Ebisu, and Tomigaya attract younger expat professionals and creatives. The ward also hosts several international schools including the British School in Tokyo (Taishido campus) and the International School of the Sacred Heart (Hiroo). Good access to the Yamanote Line, Den-en-toshi Line, and Hibiya Line. Rents are high.

rows.title: Shinjuku-ku
rows.summary: Major transit hub; diverse, mixed residential and commercial, convenient for all of Tokyo.
rows.body: Shinjuku is Tokyo's busiest railway hub and a major commercial and entertainment centre. For expats, the Nishi-Shinjuku and Yotsuya areas offer more residential and quieter living options. The ward is highly diverse, home to the famous Shinjuku 2-chome LGBTQ+ district and the sprawling Kabukicho entertainment area. Convenient for reaching all parts of Tokyo due to Shinjuku Station serving more than a dozen rail lines. Mid-range to premium rents depending on the sub-area.

rows.title: Meguro-ku
rows.summary: Residential ward; Nakameguro canal, trendy cafés, younger expats, mid-premium.
rows.body: Meguro-ku is a predominantly residential ward with strong appeal to younger expats and professionals. The Nakameguro canal is lined with cherry trees, galleries, boutiques, and stylish cafés that are particularly popular in spring. The ward also includes Jiyugaoka, known for its European café culture and upscale shopping. Good Tokyu and Tokyo Metro connections. Canadian International School Tokyo (CIS) has a Nakameguro campus here. Rents are mid-to-premium range.

rows.title: Setagaya-ku
rows.summary: Large suburban ward; family-friendly, Shakujii-koen Park area, quieter, mid-range.
rows.body: Setagaya-ku is Tokyo's most populous ward and one of its most desirable for families. The area offers a quieter, more suburban atmosphere compared to central wards, with large parks (Kinuta, Komazawa Olympic Park), excellent schools, and a strong community spirit. Popular neighbourhoods include Sangenjaya (vibrant local dining), Shimokitazawa (bohemian arts scene), and Futako-Tamagawa (riverside shopping). Rents are more affordable than Minato or Shibuya. Well connected by the Den-en-toshi and Odakyu lines.

rows.title: Nerima-ku
rows.summary: Western Tokyo suburb; residential, Shakujii-koen park, affordable, American School in Japan nearby.
rows.body: Nerima-ku is located in western Tokyo and is one of the more affordable wards in the 23-ward area. Offers a quieter, suburban lifestyle with large parks including Shakujii-koen. Nerima is well-positioned for access to the American School in Japan (ASIJ) in neighbouring Chofu City. Popular with American expat families attending ASIJ. Served by the Seibu Ikebukuro and Seibu Yurakucho lines. Lower rents than central wards make it attractive for families on mid-range budgets.

rows.title: Bunkyo-ku
rows.summary: Academic ward; University of Tokyo, residential, green, cultural institutions.
rows.body: Bunkyo-ku is home to the University of Tokyo (Hongo campus) and several other major universities, giving the area an academic and intellectual character. It is a quiet, predominantly residential ward with beautiful parks including Koishikawa Korakuen Garden and Rikugien Garden. Popular with academics, researchers, and families who value proximity to cultural institutions. Good subway access via the Tokyo Metro Marunouchi and Namboku lines. Mid-range rents by Tokyo standards.

rows.title: Sumida / Koto (East Tokyo)
rows.summary: East Tokyo modern development; Tokyo Skytree area, newer housing, waterfront, mid-range.
rows.body: Sumida and Koto wards form much of eastern central Tokyo, an area that has seen major redevelopment in recent decades. Tokyo Skytree, Japan's tallest structure, dominates the skyline. The waterfront areas along the Sumidagawa and Tokyo Bay offer newer high-rise residential developments at lower prices than west-of-river wards. Increasingly popular with younger families and those working in Marunouchi or Shinjuku who want more space for less. Good access via the Toei Asakusa Line and Yurikamome monorail.

rows.title: Edogawa / Katsushika (Outer East Tokyo)
rows.summary: Outer east Tokyo; very local, affordable, large parks, Disneyland proximity.
rows.body: Edogawa and Katsushika are outer eastern wards of Tokyo that retain a very local, traditional Japanese character with relatively few foreign residents. However, they offer some of the most affordable rents in the 23-ward area and large parks such as Kasai Rinkai Park (with access to Tokyo Disneyland in neighbouring Urayasu, Chiba). The Keiyo and Sobu Lines connect the area to central Tokyo in 30–40 minutes. A budget-friendly option for expats comfortable with a more local Japanese-language environment.

rows.title: Nakameguro / Daikanyama (Meguro-ku/Shibuya-ku)
rows.summary: Upscale, trendy canal-side neighbourhoods; creative expats, boutiques, restaurants.
rows.body: Nakameguro and Daikanyama are two of Tokyo's most fashionable neighbourhoods. The Meguro River in Nakameguro is lined with boutiques, galleries, and cafés that draw a creative and stylish crowd. Daikanyama is home to the iconic Tsutaya Books complex and upscale international dining. Very popular with creative-industry expats and younger professionals. Close to Shibuya and Ebisu by train. Premium-priced but slightly below central Minato-ku rates. Limited family housing but excellent lifestyle amenities.

rows.title: Yokohama (Kanagawa Prefecture)
rows.summary: Greater Tokyo port city; lower rents, Minato Mirai waterfront, Chinatown, international schools.
rows.body: Yokohama is Japan's second-largest city and part of Greater Tokyo's metropolitan region, about 30 minutes from central Tokyo by rail (Tokaido Line or Keikyu Line). Popular expat areas include Yamate (the historic foreign settlement), Motomachi, and the waterfront Minato Mirai district. Significantly lower rents than Tokyo's central wards. Home to the Yokohama International School (YIS) and Saint Maur International School. Strong international community with long historic ties to foreign residents. A good value option for families.

rows.title: Kawasaki (Kanagawa Prefecture)
rows.summary: Commuter suburb between Tokyo and Yokohama; mid-range rents, industrial, practical.
rows.body: Kawasaki is a large city in Kanagawa Prefecture sandwiched between Tokyo and Yokohama. It is heavily industrial in its waterfront zones but has pleasant residential areas further inland. Served by the JR Tokaido and Nambu Lines, with fast connections to Shinjuku, Shibuya, and Yokohama. Rents are more affordable than Tokyo proper. Popular with families and professionals who prioritise space and budget over lifestyle amenities. Less international school infrastructure than Yokohama, but accessible to both Tokyo and Yokohama schools.

rows.title: American School in Japan (ASIJ)
rows.summary: Leading American curriculum international school; ages 3–18 (Nursery–Grade 12); Chofu.
rows.body: Located in Chofu, western Tokyo (1-1-1 Nomizu, Chofu-shi, Tokyo). Tel: +81-422-34-5300. ASIJ is a non-profit, co-educational international school serving students from Nursery (age 3) through Grade 12. Follows a broadly American curriculum with Advanced Placement (AP) courses. Approximately 1,600 students from over 50 nationalities. Annual tuition 2025–26: Nursery–Pre-K ¥2,987,000; Kindergarten–Grade 5 ¥3,269,000; Grades 6–8 ¥3,425,000; Grades 9–12 ¥3,533,000. One-time building maintenance fee ¥1,525,000.

rows.title: The British School in Tokyo (BST)
rows.summary: Largest British international school in Japan; ages 3–18; Azabudai Hills (Primary) + Showa/Kunitachi (Secondary).
rows.body: Primary campus at 1-3-3 Azabudai, Minato-ku (Azabudai Hills); Secondary campus at 1-7-57 Taishido, Setagaya-ku (Showa campus, Kunitachi). Co-educational school for ages 3–18 following the English National Curriculum through to GCSE and A-Levels (also IB DP candidate for Years 12–13). Over 1,400 students. Annual tuition 2026–27: Primary (Nursery–Year 6) ¥2,960,000; Secondary (Year 7–9) ¥2,980,000; Secondary (Year 10–13) ¥3,070,000. Plus Capital Development Fee ¥100,000.

rows.title: Canadian International School Tokyo (CIS)
rows.summary: Canadian curriculum international school; ages 4–18; Kitashinagawa, Shinagawa-ku.
rows.body: Main campus at 5-8-20 Kita-Shinagawa, Shinagawa-ku, Tokyo 141-0001. Tel: +81-3-5793-1392. Also a Nakameguro campus (Meguro-ku). Co-educational day school offering pre-Kindergarten through Grade 12. Follows the Canadian/British Columbia curriculum with IB frameworks. Annual tuition 2025–26: Kindergarten approximately ¥2,350,000; higher grades up to ¥2,600,000–¥3,100,000. Founded 2000. Strong project-based learning approach.

rows.title: Nishimachi International School
rows.summary: Intimate bilingual international school; Kindergarten–Grade 9 (ages 5–15); Moto-Azabu, Minato-ku.
rows.body: Located at 2-14-7 Moto-Azabu, Minato-ku, Tokyo 106-0046. Tel: +81-(0)3-3451-5520. Founded 1949. Offers Kindergarten through Grade 9 (ages 5–14). American curriculum with strong emphasis on Japanese language and culture — daily Japanese classes for all students. Approximately 468 students, 1:7 student-to-teacher ratio. Average 20 students per class. An intimate, community-focused school beloved by expat families seeking a bilingual environment. 100% of graduates complete higher education.

rows.title: International School of the Sacred Heart (ISSH)
rows.summary: Catholic girls' K–12 school (co-ed Kindergarten 3–4); ages 3–18; Hiroo, Shibuya-ku.
rows.body: Located at 4-3-1 Hiroo, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo 150-0012. Tel: +81-3-3400-3951. Founded 1908; Tokyo's leading school for girls. Kindergarten 3 and 4 are co-educational; Grades 1–12 are girls only. American-based curriculum with AP courses. Annual tuition 2026–27: Kindergarten 3–4 ¥2,560,000; Kindergarten 5 ¥2,680,000; Grades 1–8 ¥2,770,000; Grades 9–11 ¥2,790,000; Grade 12 ¥2,880,000. Plus one-time Registration Fee ¥300,000 and Education & Building Development Fee ¥600,000.

rows.title: Tokyo International Learning Community (TILC)
rows.summary: Small specialist school supporting children with learning differences; Chofu area.
rows.body: Located in the Chofu area, western Tokyo (2-51-7, postcode 183-0002; Tel: 042-401-0585). TILC is a small, specialist English-medium school that supports children with learning difficulties and diverse learning needs, typically ages 4–12. Provides structured, individualized learning support. Part of the TELL Japan network supporting expat community mental health and education. A valuable resource for expat families whose children need additional learning support in the Tokyo area.

rows.title: Saint Maur International School
rows.summary: Oldest international school in Asia; Montessori–Grade 12; ages 2.5–18; Yokohama.
rows.body: Located in Yokohama, Kanagawa (accessible from Tokyo in ~30 min). Established in 1872, making it the oldest existing international school in Asia. Co-educational from age 2.5 through Grade 12. Offers Montessori Preschool (ages 2.5–5), IPC-based Elementary (ages 5/6–10/11), and IGCSE (Grades 9–10), IB Diploma Programme (Grades 11–12). Annual tuition approximately ¥3,036,000–¥3,859,000 depending on year level. English-medium instruction; Japanese language offered.

rows.title: Yokohama International School (YIS)
rows.summary: Leading IB World School; ages 3–18 (ELC–Grade 12); Naka-ku, Yokohama.
rows.body: Located at 2-100-1 Kominato-cho, Naka-ku, Yokohama 231-0802. Tel: +81(0)45-622-0084. Offers the full IB continuum from Early Learning Center (age 3) through Grade 12. Annual tuition 2026–27: ELC Half-Day ¥2,120,000; ELC Full-Day ¥2,610,000; Kindergarten–Grade 5 ¥3,210,000; Grades 6–11 ¥3,345,000; Grade 12 ¥3,440,000. Plus Campus Development Fee ¥399,000. One-time Registration Fee ¥1,480,000. Bus service available to/from Roppongi, Hiroo, and Azabu-Juban areas in Tokyo. CIS-accredited.

rows.title: North Shore Lower — Neutral Bay, Cremorne, Mosman
rows.summary: Prestige harbour-side living immediately north of the bridge. Quiet leafy streets, boutique village shopping strips, and direct ferry access to the CBD make this the first choice for senior corporate expats.
rows.body: The Lower North Shore sits between the Harbour Bridge and the Lane Cove River, encompassing Neutral Bay, Cremorne, Mosman, and Kirribilli. Properties range from Art Deco apartments near Military Road to freestanding Federation homes with water glimpses. The area is served by the B-Line bus corridor and multiple ferry wharves (Neutral Bay, Cremorne, Mosman). Mosman hosts several elite private schools (Queenwood, SCEGGS campus) and is within catchment of North Sydney Boys and Girls Selective High Schools. Restaurants and cafés cluster around Military Road and the village centres. Median weekly rent for a 2-bedroom apartment sits around AUD 900–1 000/week in 2026.

rows.title: Eastern Suburbs — Bondi Beach, Coogee, Randwick
rows.summary: Sydney's iconic beachside belt with a vibrant café culture, ocean pools, and a strong UK, Irish, and South African expat community. Great lifestyle balance between beach and city.
rows.body: The Eastern Suburbs arc from Bondi Beach south through Tamarama, Bronte, Coogee, and Randwick. The corridor is dominated by 1930s–1960s apartment blocks, terrace houses, and newer boutique developments. Randwick is the site of UNSW Sydney, Prince of Wales Hospital, and the Royal Randwick Racecourse. Public transport connects via the T4 Eastern Suburbs Railway to Town Hall in under 20 minutes. Coogee and Randwick attract families priced out of Bondi but still wanting beach access. Bondi itself is Sydney's most internationally recognised suburb with a median 2BR unit rent of approximately AUD 850/week in 2026. The area has a dense supply of cafés, coastal walks, and weekend markets.

rows.title: Inner West — Balmain, Leichhardt, Newtown
rows.summary: Creative village neighbourhoods with strong community identity, excellent cafés and restaurants, and good transport links. Popular with young professionals, academics, and families seeking a cosmopolitan but unpretentious atmosphere.
rows.body: The Inner West encompasses Balmain, Rozelle, Leichhardt, Newtown, Marrickville, and Dulwich Hill. The area is defined by Victorian terrace houses, renovated workers' cottages, and a strong arts and hospitality scene centred on King Street (Newtown) and Norton Street (Leichhardt). The Inner West Light Rail connects Dulwich Hill to Central, and the Metro West (Marrickville station) opened in 2025, cutting commutes significantly. Newtown hosts the University of Sydney overflow population and has one of Sydney's most diverse dining strips. Rents are mid-range relative to the Eastern Suburbs and North Shore, with 2BR units around AUD 620/week in Newtown. The suburb is walkable, dog-friendly, and strong on independent bookstores, live music, and farmer's markets.

rows.title: North Shore Upper — Killara, Gordon, Lindfield
rows.summary: Quiet, leafy Upper North Shore suburbs beloved by families for outstanding private and selective state schools, generous block sizes, and a relaxed suburban pace with train access to the CBD.
rows.body: The Upper North Shore runs along the T1 North Shore railway line from Roseville through Lindfield, Killara, Gordon, and Pymble. Wide tree-lined streets, large family homes with gardens, and proximity to top private schools (Pymble Ladies College, Knox Grammar) define the character. The train to Wynyard (CBD) takes around 30–40 minutes. Gordon and Killara have village-style shopping strips. Properties are predominantly freestanding houses ranging from Federation-era to 1970s brick. Average rent for a 3BR house runs around AUD 750–900/week. The suburb cluster is considered one of the safest and most stable family markets in Greater Sydney. Expat families typically remain in this precinct for the duration of corporate assignments due to school continuity.

rows.title: Northern Beaches — Manly, Dee Why, Narrabeen
rows.summary: A coastal paradise stretching 30 km north of the Harbour, famous for surf beaches, national parks, and a relaxed outdoor lifestyle. Popular with families and surfers who trade CBD proximity for ocean living.
rows.body: The Northern Beaches peninsula runs from Manly (accessible by 30-minute ferry from Circular Quay) north through Dee Why, Collaroy, Narrabeen, Mona Vale, to Palm Beach. Manly itself is a compact beach town with a thriving restaurant scene and fast ferry to the CBD. Dee Why and Narrabeen offer larger family homes at lower price points than Manly. Public transport relies heavily on the B-Line express bus to the city; travel times are 45–70 minutes. Rents for 2BR units average AUD 750–900/week across the peninsula. The area attracts a large international expat community, particularly from the UK and New Zealand, drawn by the outdoor lifestyle, good international school options, and strong community spirit.

rows.title: CBD and Barangaroo
rows.summary: Sydney's corporate core and waterfront precinct. Home to the ASX, major law and finance firms, and premium apartment towers with harbour views. Ideal for executives who prioritise a zero-commute lifestyle.
rows.body: The Sydney CBD and adjacent Barangaroo precinct occupy the western waterfront of the peninsula. Barangaroo is a 22-hectare urban renewal project completed in stages from 2015–2023, featuring Crown Sydney, Salesforce Tower, and a waterfront promenade. The CBD is serviced by every heavy rail line, multiple bus routes, light rail, and the future Sydney Metro City & Southwest. Apartment supply is dense; typical 2BR apartments in Barangaroo command AUD 1 000–1 400/week. The area is predominantly adult-oriented with limited family housing, though some premium buildings have playgrounds and pools. Walsh Bay and Millers Point provide heritage alternatives at the northern edge. Walking distance to Opera House, Darling Harbour, and ferry terminals.

rows.title: Hills District — Castle Hill, Baulkham Hills, Norwest
rows.summary: Sydney's outer north-west growth corridor with newer housing estates, excellent Catholic and independent schools, strong community infrastructure, and growing Metro connectivity. A popular choice for families seeking space and value.
rows.body: The Hills District spans Castle Hill, Baulkham Hills, Rouse Hill, and the Norwest business park. The Sydney Metro Northwest (Northwest Metro Line) opened in 2019, connecting Norwest and Hills Showground to Chatswood and the CBD in under 40 minutes. The area is characterised by newer townhouses, semi-detached homes, and estate developments with parks and sporting facilities. Notable schools include Hills Grammar, Gilroy Catholic College, and Loretto Kirribilli's sibling school in the area. Rents are among Sydney's most competitive for family-sized properties: a 3–4BR house averages AUD 650–800/week. Popular with Asian Australian families and international migrants. Norwest is a major business hub with Norwest Marketown and the Baulkham Hills town centre.

rows.title: Sutherland Shire and Cronulla
rows.summary: Sydney's southern coastal fringe, anchored by Cronulla Beach — the only ocean beach reachable by train. Family-oriented, beach-focused, and notably more affordable than the Eastern Suburbs or Northern Beaches.
rows.body: The Sutherland Shire encompasses Cronulla, Caringbah, Miranda, Gymea, and Sutherland. The T4 Eastern Suburbs & Illawarra Line terminates at Cronulla, offering a direct 65-minute ride to the City. Cronulla Beach is a flagship lifestyle drawcard. The shire is predominantly detached house suburban, with significant national park fringe (Royal National Park borders the shire to the south). Schools include Aquinas Catholic College, Sutherland Shire Christian School, and several well-regarded state high schools. Rents for 3BR houses sit around AUD 650–800/week. The population is predominantly Anglo-Australian with a growing international community. Miranda Fair is the primary regional shopping centre.

rows.title: Parramatta and Greater Western Sydney
rows.summary: Sydney's geographic centre and fastest-growing economic hub. Affordable, highly diverse, and rapidly improving in amenity through large infrastructure investment including Sydney Metro West and WestConnex.
rows.body: Parramatta is designated as Sydney's second CBD and sits 23 km west of the city centre. It hosts Westmead Hospital precinct, Parramatta Park (World Heritage), Western Sydney University, and major government offices. The T1 Western Line and Parramatta Light Rail provide city links. The Metro West (under construction, due 2030) will cut journey times to Wynyard to under 20 minutes. The broader Western Sydney region includes Rydalmere, Harris Park, and Granville. Rents are Sydney's most affordable for large properties: 3BR houses average AUD 500–650/week. The area is the primary landing zone for new migrants from South Asia, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Parramatta Stadium and Riverside Theatres provide major entertainment infrastructure.

rows.title: Chatswood and Lane Cove
rows.summary: Mid-North Shore hub with a prominent East Asian community, excellent dining, direct rail and metro links to the CBD, and a growing apartment stock. A practical base for families and professionals.
rows.body: Chatswood is 9 km north of the CBD on the T1 North Shore Line and the Sydney Metro Northwest. The town centre is a compact, high-density retail and restaurant precinct dominated by East Asian cuisine and supermarkets (Chatswood Chase, Westfield). Lane Cove to the south offers quieter village living with lower-density housing. Rents for 2BR apartments in Chatswood sit around AUD 750–850/week; Lane Cove houses command AUD 800–1 000/week. The suburb has a significant Chinese, Korean, and Japanese expat community, with access to the Sydney Japanese Language School (Saturday school). Good state schools and proximity to North Sydney private schools.

rows.title: St Leonards and Crows Nest
rows.summary: A medical and professional precinct on the Lower North Shore, undergoing rapid urban renewal with new Metro station, hotel and apartment towers, and improving café and restaurant culture.
rows.body: St Leonards sits at the junction of the T1 North Shore Line and the Sydney Metro City & Southwest (Victoria Cross and St Leonards stations). The suburb is anchored by Royal North Shore Hospital, one of NSW's largest tertiary hospitals, and associated medical education precinct. Crows Nest to the north is a flat-land village with Crows Nest Village Centre, cafe culture, and low-rise residential streets. Rents for 2BR apartments range AUD 700–850/week. The area attracts medical professionals, healthcare workers, and corporate tenants. Close proximity to Neutral Bay, Chatswood, and North Sydney makes it a well-positioned mid-point. Limited family housing but excellent transport and growing amenity.

rows.title: Macquarie Park and Ryde
rows.summary: A tech and education hub anchored by Macquarie University, hosting major technology and pharmaceutical campuses. Diverse, mid-range, and well-connected via Metro.
rows.body: Macquarie Park is centred on Macquarie University and the Macquarie Shopping Centre. Major employers include Microsoft, Optus, Cochlear, and CSIRO. The Sydney Metro Northwest Macquarie University station provides a 35-minute ride to the CBD. Ryde is the broader Local Government Area and is one of Sydney's most multicultural suburbs, with large Korean, Chinese, and Indian communities. Rents for 2BR apartments range AUD 620–750/week. Victoria Avenue in North Ryde and Ryde itself offer villa-style units and townhouses suitable for families. The suburb is popular with Macquarie University students and researchers, tech workers, and expat professionals at nearby corporate campuses.

rows.title: International Grammar School (IGS) Sydney
rows.summary: Sydney's leading secular IB school from Preschool to Year 12. Multilingual focus (French, Italian, Spanish, Japanese, Chinese), strong performing arts, and genuinely inclusive culture make it ideal for internationally mobile families.
rows.body: IGS is located in Ultimo, a short walk from the CBD. It offers the IB Primary Years Programme (PYP), Middle Years Programme (MYP), and Diploma Programme (DP), making it one of Sydney's few end-to-end IB schools. The school is co-educational, non-religious, and explicitly international in outlook. Languages of instruction include English alongside French, Italian, and Japanese streams from early years. Annual fees range from approximately AUD 12 000 (Preschool) to AUD 28 000 (Year 12 Diploma). The school has waiting lists, particularly for the French bilingual stream. ATAR equivalent results are competitive. Enrolment is approx 1 100 students.

rows.title: Shore School (Sydney Church of England Grammar School)
rows.summary: One of Sydney's most prestigious Anglican boys' schools on the Lower North Shore, known for academic rigour, strong rowing and rugby traditions, and significant old boys' network in law, finance, and medicine.
rows.body: Shore School is located in North Sydney on the Lower North Shore, founded in 1889. The school caters to boys from Year 7 to Year 12 (with a Junior School from Kindergarten to Year 6). Annual fees are approximately AUD 35 000–40 000 for senior day students. Shore is not a full IB school but offers the HSC (Higher School Certificate); it consistently ranks in the top 10–15 NSW schools by ATAR performance. Boarding is available. The campus overlooks Sydney Harbour and includes extensive sporting facilities. The school has a strong international student community and an alumni network that reaches into ASX boardrooms.

rows.title: SCEGGS Darlinghurst
rows.summary: A leading Anglican girls' school in central Sydney offering HSC and IB Diploma. Strong STEM and arts programme, diverse student body, and exceptional CBD proximity make it popular with expat families.
rows.body: SCEGGS (Sydney Church of England Girls Grammar School) is located in Darlinghurst, minutes from the CBD. Founded in 1895, it offers education from Kindergarten to Year 12 and is one of the few Sydney girls' schools offering both the HSC and the IB Diploma. Fees range from approximately AUD 30 000–40 000 per year for senior students. The school has a diverse intake including many international families. The campus has recently undergone a major redevelopment including new STEM and performing arts facilities. Co-curricular strength includes debating, music, and rowing.

rows.title: Cranbrook School
rows.summary: Sydney's most expensive private school, an Anglican boys' school in Bellevue Hill offering both the HSC and IB Diploma. Exceptional facilities, outstanding ATAR results, and Australia's highest Year 12 tuition fees.
rows.body: Cranbrook School is located in Bellevue Hill in the Eastern Suburbs, founded in 1918. It is consistently ranked among Australia's top three schools by ATAR performance. The school is co-educational at junior level (to Year 6) and boys-only from Year 7. Annual senior day school fees reached AUD 49 521 in 2025, making it the most expensive day school in Australia. The school offers both HSC and IB Diploma Programme. Campus facilities include an aquatic centre, cricket oval, art studios, and a performing arts centre. Strong boarding provision for interstate and international students. The old boys' network is deeply embedded in Sydney's professional elite.

rows.title: Knox Grammar School
rows.summary: A large, high-performing Presbyterian boys' school on the Upper North Shore offering the IB Diploma and HSC. Exceptional sporting tradition, outstanding ATAR and IB results, and strong international boarding programme.
rows.body: Knox Grammar School is located in Wahroonga on the Upper North Shore, founded in 1895. The school operates from Early Learning to Year 12 and is co-educational at ELC/Junior level and boys-only from Year 7. Knox is one of NSW's largest non-government schools with approximately 2 200 students. It offers both the IB Diploma Programme and HSC at senior level. Annual fees are approximately AUD 35 000–40 000 for day students; international student boarding fees are considerably higher. The school has an extensive boarding facility that attracts students from across Asia-Pacific. Sporting infrastructure includes multiple ovals, an aquatic centre, and tennis courts.

rows.title: UNSW Global
rows.summary: The university-level pathway for international students joining the University of New South Wales. Offers foundation, diploma, and English language programmes aligned to UNSW undergraduate entry.
rows.body: UNSW Global is the international admissions and pathway arm of the University of New South Wales, ranked consistently in the top 50 universities worldwide. It operates foundation year programmes, postgraduate enabling programmes, and English language programmes from its Kensington campus adjacent to UNSW Sydney. The University itself spans Engineering, Law, Business, Medicine, and Arts. UNSW Global is particularly well-regarded among students from China, India, South Korea, and Southeast Asia. Annual tuition for undergraduate programmes ranges from AUD 40 000–55 000 depending on faculty. The Kensington campus is 7 km from the CBD, well served by buses and the T4 light rail.

rows.title: Lycée Condorcet — International French School of Sydney
rows.summary: The only French government-affiliated school in NSW, in Maroubra. Offers the French National Curriculum and three Baccalaureate options including the IB. Essential for French expat families and those seeking a French-language education.
rows.body: Lycée Condorcet is located at 758 Anzac Parade, Maroubra, in the Eastern Suburbs. Founded in 1965, it is accredited by the French Ministry of Education and administered under the AEFE (Agency for French Education Abroad) network. The school offers preschool through to Year 12 (Terminale), delivering the French National Curriculum in French. Three Baccalaureate options are available: the French Baccalaureate, the International Baccalaureate Diploma (IBDP), and the OIB (Option Internationale du Baccalaureat). Annual fees are approximately AUD 12 000–18 000, making it significantly more affordable than comparable private schools. Strong community of French, Belgian, Swiss, and Francophone African families.

rows.title: Yorkville, Rosedale and Moore Park
rows.summary: Toronto's most prestigious inner-city neighbourhood cluster — ultra-premium residential streets, high-end retail and dining, and a quiet grandeur favoured by executives, diplomats, and established wealth.
rows.body: Yorkville sits at Bloor Street and Avenue Road, characterised by boutique designer shops, high-end hotels (Four Seasons, Hazelton), and fine-dining restaurants. Rosedale and Moore Park extend north across the ravine into quiet, tree-lined residential streets of Victorian and Edwardian homes. The area is served by Bloor-Yonge subway station, one of the system's busiest interchanges, providing rapid access across the city. Average rent for a 2BR apartment in Yorkville ranges CAD 4 000–5 500/month; Rosedale townhouses command CAD 5 500–7 500/month. The neighbourhood has a small-town feel within a global city. Private members' clubs (York Club, National Club) are nearby. Rosedale Public School and Forest Hill Collegiate are strong local options.

rows.title: Forest Hill and Lawrence Park
rows.summary: Wealthy residential enclaves north of Midtown Toronto, home to Canada's top private schools including UCC and Bishop Strachan. Generous properties, ravine lots, and a stable, family-oriented atmosphere.
rows.body: Forest Hill and Lawrence Park occupy the swath of Midtown Toronto between Bathurst Street and Yonge Street, north of Eglinton. Forest Hill Village has a charming commercial strip with bakeries, delis, and boutiques. The neighbourhood is famous for hosting Upper Canada College and Bishop Strachan School on adjacent campuses. Lawrence Park is the quieter, more residential complement to the north. Properties are primarily large single-family detached homes, many with ravine or park views. Rents for 3BR houses range CAD 4 500–7 000/month. Access to the Eglinton Crosstown LRT (opened 2024) has improved east-west connections. A predominantly Jewish community in parts of Forest Hill; Lawrence Park tends toward established Anglo-Canadian families.

rows.title: The Annex and Bloor West Village
rows.summary: Vibrant, walkable Midtown neighbourhoods adjacent to the University of Toronto. Eclectic mix of academics, professionals, and families. Excellent transit, bookshops, restaurants, and cultural institutions.
rows.body: The Annex runs along Bloor Street West between Spadina Avenue and Bathurst Street, north toward Dupont. It is defined by Victorian and Edwardian detached homes, many converted to student or professional rentals. The neighbourhood is shaped by the University of Toronto's St George campus, with OISE, Robarts Library, and the ROM (Royal Ontario Museum) within walking distance. Bloor-Spadina subway station provides city-wide connectivity. Bloor West Village, further west toward High Park, adds a more family-oriented commercial strip with European delis and cafés. Rents for 2BR apartments range CAD 2 800–3 800/month; 3BR houses CAD 3 500–5 000. A strong progressive community ethos.

rows.title: King West and Liberty Village
rows.summary: Toronto's creative and tech district. Condo-heavy, restaurant-rich, and dominated by young professionals. King Street is a global benchmark for car-free transit pilot programmes and a thriving nightlife corridor.
rows.body: King West and Liberty Village sit west of the downtown core, between Bathurst and Dufferin streets. King Street West is lined with restaurants, cocktail bars, patios, and boutique retail. Liberty Village, immediately south, is a reclaimed Victorian industrial estate now densely packed with condo towers, creative agencies, and co-working spaces. Major employers include tech scale-ups, media companies, and advertising agencies. The King streetcar (504) is the primary transit artery. Rents for 2BR condos average CAD 2 800–3 500/month. The demographic is predominantly 25–40 childless professionals, but families with young children are present. Limited green space but proximity to Trinity Bellwoods Park.

rows.title: Distillery District and St. Lawrence Market
