rows.summary: Historic east-downtown neighbourhoods combining Victorian industrial architecture, a world-class food market, art galleries, and a rapidly growing residential base. Well positioned for those working in downtown financial core.
rows.body: The Distillery District is a National Historic Site at Parliament and Mill Streets, comprising 44 buildings of Victorian-era industrial architecture now housing restaurants, galleries, artisan shops, and condos. The weekly Christmas Market is internationally famous. St. Lawrence Market, a short walk west, has operated since 1803 and is rated one of the world's best food markets. The area sits between King and Front Streets, immediately east of the financial district. The King streetcar and forthcoming Ontario Line subway (planned 2027) improve connectivity. 2BR condos in the district average CAD 3 000–4 000/month. A growing arts and young-professional community; limited family-size housing.

rows.title: Leslieville and East End
rows.summary: An arts-driven, family-friendly east-end neighbourhood with a strong community market, independent restaurants, and a growing number of young families attracted by relatively affordable house prices.
rows.body: Leslieville runs along Queen Street East between Broadview and Leslie streets. Once a working-class industrial area, it has gentrified steadily since the early 2000s and is now defined by vintage shops, brunch restaurants, and a strong community market scene. The east end includes Riverdale, Playter Estates, and Danforth Village. The area is served by the Queen and Broadview streetcars and Donlands, Greenwood, and Pape TTC subway stations. Rents for 3BR houses average CAD 3 200–4 200/month. Strong local school options include Earl Haig PS and Riverdale Collegiate. The neighbourhood is a popular destination for artists, queer families, and young parents priced out of the Annex or King West.

rows.title: North York — Yonge and Sheppard
rows.summary: Toronto's northern suburban core with a significant Korean and Asian community, a dense condo market, and excellent subway/bus connectivity to downtown. Practical and affordable relative to midtown.
rows.body: North York is centred on the Yonge-Sheppard intersection, where two subway lines (Yonge-University and Sheppard) intersect. The area is dense with high-rise condos and mid-rise apartment towers. Mel Lastman Square provides public space and Civic Centre services. A large Korean community clusters around Yonge Street north of Sheppard, with Korean supermarkets, restaurants, and banks. Average rent for a 2BR condo is CAD 2 500–3 200/month. Quick subway ride to downtown (about 25 minutes to Bloor). Strong public schools in catchment. Popular with corporate assignees from Korean chaebols and Japanese multinationals with Toronto offices. The Sheppard Avenue East LRT (planned) will improve east-west connections.

rows.title: Etobicoke and Humber Bay
rows.summary: Toronto's western lakefront suburbs offering mid-range condos and family homes with waterfront access. Popular with families and professionals who want lake views without downtown prices.
rows.body: Etobicoke is the western borough of the City of Toronto, encompassing neighbourhoods from Rexdale in the north to Humber Bay Shores in the south. Humber Bay Shores is a fast-growing waterfront condo district with direct lake access, cycling trails, and parkland. The Mimico and Long Branch areas offer affordable detached houses. Transit connections include the Bloor-Danforth subway (Kipling terminus) and GO Train. Rents for 2BR condos in Humber Bay average CAD 2 600–3 200/month; family houses in Etobicoke run CAD 3 000–4 000/month. The community is ethnically diverse with large South Asian, Caribbean, and Central European communities. Sherway Gardens mall provides retail.

rows.title: Mississauga — Streetsville and Port Credit
rows.summary: A separate city west of Toronto offering excellent suburban schools, lakefront living at Port Credit, and the charming village character of Streetsville — all within commuting range of downtown Toronto via GO Train.
rows.body: Mississauga is Canada's sixth-largest city and borders Toronto to the west. Port Credit is a historic fishing village on Lake Ontario, now a premium residential and restaurant destination. Streetsville, in central Mississauga, retains a heritage village feel with independent shops and a popular Christmas parade. The Lakeshore West GO Train connects Port Credit to Union Station in approximately 30 minutes. Rents for 3BR homes in Mississauga range CAD 2 800–3 800/month — significantly below equivalent Toronto neighbourhoods. Top schools include Mississauga Secondary School (IB), Port Credit SS, and a range of Catholic and independent options. Average 2BR apartment in central Mississauga: CAD 2 200–2 800/month.

rows.title: Oakville and Burlington
rows.summary: Premium suburban towns on Lake Ontario west of Mississauga, offering some of Canada's best public and private schools, generous homes with yards, and a quiet, safe small-town feel within the Greater Toronto commuter belt.
rows.body: Oakville and Burlington are adjacent lakefront municipalities 40–55 km west of downtown Toronto. Oakville consistently ranks among Canada's wealthiest municipalities by median household income. The town is known for Appleby College (elite boarding school), Oakville Trafalgar High School, and strong Catholic school board options. Burlington's Central Park area has good parkland and a vibrant arts scene. The Lakeshore West GO Train connects both towns to Union Station in 35–55 minutes. Rents for 3BR family homes range CAD 3 000–4 500/month. New housing developments offer modern townhouses and detached homes with double garages at lower per-square-foot costs than Toronto. Popular with expat families on 3–5 year assignments.

rows.title: Scarborough and Agincourt
rows.summary: Affordable, ethnically diverse eastern suburbs with improving transit links. A major landing zone for new immigrants from South Asia, China, and the Caribbean. Large detached homes at significantly below-average Toronto rents.
rows.body: Scarborough is the eastern borough of the City of Toronto. Agincourt, in the north, has a large Chinese and Taiwanese community with a dense supply of Chinese-language services, groceries, and restaurants. South Scarborough (Scarborough Bluffs) has dramatic lakefront cliffs and more affordable family housing. The Scarborough RT is being replaced by the Scarborough Subway Extension (Ontario Line, due 2030), which will significantly improve transit access. Current commute to downtown by TTC subway (Bloor-Danforth to Kennedy) takes 40–50 minutes. Rents for 3BR detached houses range CAD 2 200–3 000/month. Strong public school system with several IB schools. Popular with families prioritising space and value.

rows.title: Richmond Hill and Markham
rows.summary: Premier northern suburbs with a large, well-established Chinese community, outstanding public and private schools, newer housing stock, and highway and GO Train access to downtown Toronto.
rows.body: Richmond Hill and Markham sit in York Region, north of Toronto. Markham's Highway 7 corridor is nicknamed 'Little Hong Kong' for its dense concentration of Cantonese and Mandarin-speaking businesses, shopping centres (Pacific Mall, First Markham Place), and restaurants. Richmond Hill is quieter and more residential, with excellent Yonge Street access. Both areas have outstanding public school performance; Unionville High School (Markham) offers one of Ontario's top IB programmes. GO Train (Stouffville and Richmond Hill lines) provides downtown access in 50–70 minutes. Rents for 3BR family homes average CAD 2 800–3 800/month. Average rent data: Richmond Hill 2BR at CAD 2 680/month (Rentals.ca, 2025).

rows.title: Toronto French School (TFS)
rows.summary: Canada's oldest independent bilingual school (French-English), offering IB from Early Years to Diploma. Located in Forest Hill and North York campuses. The top choice for Francophone expat families and bilingual education seekers.
rows.body: TFS — Canada's International School was founded in 1962 and operates two campuses: the Junior School in Forest Hill and the Senior School in Don Mills (North York). It is fully bilingual French-English and offers the IB continuum (PYP, MYP, DP). The school has approximately 1 400 students from over 60 countries. Annual tuition ranges from approximately CAD 23 000 (JK) to CAD 35 000 (Grade 12). TFS has extensive international exchanges and Model UN participation. The school is a member of the League of Research Universities (via U of T partnership) and Headmasters' and Headmistresses' Conference. An exceptionally strong choice for families rotating between Paris, Geneva, Brussels, or Montreal.

rows.title: Upper Canada College (UCC)
rows.summary: Canada's most prestigious boys' school, founded 1829. Located in Forest Hill. Offers a rigorous academic programme aligned to the Ontario curriculum with strong IB Diploma results. Exceptional alumni network reaching into Canadian politics, law, and finance.
rows.body: Upper Canada College is located in Forest Hill, operating since 1829. The school serves boys from JK through Year 12 (Ontario Grade 12). Day school tuition is approximately CAD 44 940–48 720/year (2026-27). Boarding fees are CAD 81 000–87 000 (domestic/international). UCC's alumni network includes multiple prime ministers, Supreme Court justices, and corporate leaders. The school offers the Ontario Secondary School Diploma with University preparation courses and a small IB Diploma cohort. Campus facilities include a skating rink, theatre, science labs, and extensive sports fields. Boarding available from Grade 9. International enrolment approximately 15% of student body.

rows.title: The Bishop Strachan School (BSS)
rows.summary: Toronto's leading independent Anglican girls' school, adjacent to UCC in Forest Hill. Offers IB Diploma and Ontario curriculum. Known for academic excellence, leadership programming, and a strong boarding community.
rows.body: Bishop Strachan School is located adjacent to Upper Canada College in Forest Hill, making it a natural companion school in the city's premier private school cluster. BSS serves girls from JK to Grade 12. Day tuition is approximately CAD 43 800/year; boarding is CAD 82 200/year (2026-27). The school offers both the Ontario diploma and the IB Diploma Programme. BSS has a strong STEM programme for girls and a robust performing arts centre. Boarding available from Grade 9; international boarding approximately 10% of students. The school runs leadership retreats, exchange programmes to the UK and Australia, and a Global Citizenship curriculum.

rows.title: Crescent School
rows.summary: An independent boys' school in North York, offering IB Diploma alongside the Ontario curriculum. Known for its character-development ethos, strong athletics, and welcoming international student community.
rows.body: Crescent School is located in Willowdale, North York, operating since 1913. The school serves boys from Grade 3 to Grade 12 (approximately 650 students). It offers the Ontario Secondary School Diploma and, at senior level, the IB Diploma Programme. Day tuition is approximately CAD 33 000–36 000/year. The school emphasises character education ('Men of Character' programme), athletics, and community service. Campus includes a rink, theatre, and extensive playing fields. International students represent approximately 20% of enrolment. Crescent is closely affiliated with the Havergal College (sister school) for joint social events. Strong alumni in business, law, and sport.

rows.title: International School of Toronto (ISOT)
rows.summary: A full IB continuum school in Don Mills offering PYP, MYP, and DP. Genuinely international student body and highly experienced IB faculty. The natural first call for newly arriving expat families seeking curriculum continuity.
rows.body: The International School of Toronto is located in Don Mills, North York, operating since 1979. It offers the full IB continuum from Primary Years Programme (age 3) through the Diploma Programme (Grade 12). The school has approximately 500 students from over 40 countries. Annual tuition ranges from CAD 20 000 (ECC) to CAD 30 000 (DP). Small class sizes (average 15–18 students), an experienced multinational faculty, and a well-established admissions process for mid-year international arrivals distinguish ISOT from Ontario curriculum alternatives. The school shares a campus arrangement in the Don Mills area and is well connected by the Eglinton Crosstown LRT (Leaside extension). A primary choice for families from US, UK, Europe, and Asia-Pacific.

rows.title: Havergal College
rows.summary: An Anglican girls' school on Lawrence Avenue in North Toronto, offering both Ontario curriculum and IB Diploma. Strong academic results, boarding facility, and a vibrant arts and athletics programme.
rows.body: Havergal College has operated since 1894 and is located on Lawrence Avenue West, in the Lawrence Park area. The school serves girls from JK to Grade 12 (approximately 950 students). Day tuition is approximately CAD 36 000–40 000/year; boarding fees are around CAD 65 000/year. Havergal offers the Ontario Secondary School Diploma and the IB Diploma Programme. The school is noted for a high university acceptance rate to Canadian, US, and UK universities. Extensive performing arts and athletics facilities, including a new fitness centre. International students make up approximately 15% of enrolment. Closely associated with Upper Canada College through joint programmes.

rows.title: Greenwood College School
rows.summary: A progressive co-educational independent school at Yonge and St. Clair offering the Ontario curriculum with a strong inquiry-based, student-centred approach. Ideal for families seeking a less traditional, highly engaged school culture.
rows.body: Greenwood College School is located at Yonge Street and St. Clair Avenue, making it one of the most centrally located independent schools in Toronto (Davisville subway station steps away). The school serves students from Grade 7 to Grade 12 (approximately 350 students). Annual tuition is approximately CAD 26 000–29 000/year. Greenwood does not offer the IB Diploma but delivers the Ontario curriculum through project-based learning, design thinking, and student-driven inquiry. The school has strong university placement results (85%+ to top Canadian and US universities). Small class sizes and an exceptionally close student-teacher relationship define the culture. Popular with families from creative, tech, and academic professions.

rows.title: Frogner (incl. Skillebekk, Aker Brygge / Tjuvholmen)
rows.summary: Oslo's most prestigious west-side district: embassies, grand apartment blocks, Vigeland Park — and the district French-corridor families gravitate to.
rows.body: Frogner is the traditional upper-west side of Oslo and the borough most associated with diplomats and international executives. It runs from Skillebekk and Solli plass up past the Vigeland sculpture park, and administratively also covers the Aker Brygge and Tjuvholmen waterfront. Housing stock is late-19th-century apartment buildings with high ceilings and few lifts. It is the single most relevant district for the France→Norway corridor: the French embassy sits on Drammensveien, and the Lycée français René Cassin's primary and lower-secondary site is at Skovveien 9 in the middle of the district. Rents are the highest in the city — a 2-bedroom runs about NOK 22,000–30,000/month on a first-hand contract and NOK 25,000–34,000 on a sublet, with 3-bedrooms NOK 30,000–48,000. Around 12 minutes to the centre by tram (lines 12/13/19). Best for senior assignees, diplomatic households and French-schooling families who want to walk to school; least suited to anyone optimising for space per krone.

extras.research_note: Rent bands are the AffordWhere Oslo dataset compiled from official statistics in January 2026; corroborated by Investropa's early-2026 Oslo rent survey (2BR city average about NOK 24,000, premium districts NOK 22,000–28,000 rising above NOK 30,000 for renovated units).
extras.corridor_relevance: FR-NO / NO-FR — French embassy on Drammensveien and the LFO Skovveien 9 site are both in this district

rows.title: Majorstuen & Uranienborg
rows.summary: Transit hub with an established international population; premium but slightly cheaper than Frogner proper.
rows.body: Majorstuen is where five tram lines, the T-bane and a dense retail strip (Bogstadveien) meet, which makes it the most practical premium address in Oslo. Uranienborg immediately south is quieter and residential. The area is consistently named among the districts most popular with expatriates and with young professionals, and it is a 10–15 minute walk or one tram stop from the LFO Skovveien site. Two-bedroom rents sit around NOK 22,000–28,000/month, with the top of the band for renovated flats. Everything a new arrival needs — pharmacies, a Vinmonopolet, gyms, English-speaking GP practices — is within walking distance, and the T-bane reaches both the Bjørvika business district and the Holmenkollen ski area in under 20 minutes. Good compromise district for a first Oslo posting.

extras.research_note: Investropa (early 2026): 'The three Oslo neighborhoods most popular with expats are Frogner, Majorstuen, and St. Hanshaugen.'
extras.corridor_relevance: FR-NO — walking distance to the LFO Skovveien site; named among the three districts most popular with expats

rows.title: St. Hanshaugen & Bislett
rows.summary: Central, walkable and residential — the third district expats consistently pick, with a large hilltop park.
rows.body: St. Hanshaugen wraps around the park of the same name, between the university quarter and Sagene. Bislett, on its eastern edge, is built around the athletics stadium. The appeal is walkability: the centre, Grünerløkka and Majorstuen are all 10–20 minutes on foot, so a household can function without a car and without long tram rides. Housing is mostly pre-war apartment blocks, with a mix of student, professional and family occupancy that keeps the area lively year-round. Two-bedroom rents are in the upper-middle band — broadly NOK 20,000–26,000/month — and the district is repeatedly listed alongside Frogner and Majorstuen as an expat favourite. Suited to couples and small families who value being central over having a garden.

extras.research_note: Rent band interpolated from the Investropa early-2026 Oslo range (city 2BR average about NOK 24,000; premium districts NOK 22,000–28,000; mid-range NOK 16,000–20,000) — treat as an indicative band, not a quoted figure.

rows.title: Grünerløkka
rows.summary: Oslo's most vibrant district and the usual landing spot for internationals arriving without children.
rows.body: Grünerløkka — 'Løkka' — is the former working-class quarter along the Akerselva river that became Oslo's café, bar and independent-retail district. It is the neighbourhood most often recommended to arriving internationals: dense, walkable, well served by trams and the T-bane, and about 10 minutes from the centre. Rents are noticeably below the west side: 2-bedrooms at roughly NOK 18,000–24,000/month on a first-hand contract and NOK 21,000–27,000 on a sublet, 1-bedrooms from about NOK 13,000. The Vulkan development on the western edge — Mathallen food hall, Dansens Hus — is also where the Lycée français runs its upper-secondary site (Vulkan 11), which makes Løkka unexpectedly practical for French families with teenagers. Trade-offs: weekend noise on the main streets and little green space beyond the river path.

extras.research_note: Rent bands: AffordWhere Oslo dataset, official statistics compiled January 2026. LFO dual-site confirmed on lfo.no/contact (Skovveien 9 and Vulkan 11).
extras.corridor_relevance: FR-NO — the LFO upper-secondary site is at Vulkan 11, on the western edge of this district

rows.title: Sagene & Torshov
rows.summary: Quieter northern extension of Grünerløkka; better value, increasingly popular with young families.
rows.body: Sagene and Torshov sit just north of Grünerløkka along the Akerselva. The same period housing stock and tram access, with more parks (Torshovparken, Bjølsen), fewer bars and lower rents — which is why the district keeps appearing on lists of areas popular with young professionals and with families who want to stay on the east side. Expect 2-bedrooms in the NOK 17,000–23,000/month range. Nydalen, one stop further north on the T-bane, is a modern office cluster (BI Norwegian Business School) that makes Sagene a short commute for anyone working there. Practical, unpretentious district; the main compromise is that international-school runs to Bekkestua or Skådalen mean crossing the city.

extras.research_note: Characterisation from the LifeX Oslo expat rental guide ('Sagene / Torshov — slightly further north, increasingly popular, slightly more affordable'); rent band interpolated from the Investropa early-2026 bands.

rows.title: Skøyen & Ullern
rows.summary: Western business-and-family belt: corporate offices at Skøyen, quiet residential streets in Ullern.
rows.body: Skøyen is a major office node on the western rail and tram corridor, and Ullern is the residential borough above it — detached houses, low-rise apartments, good schools and Oslo's highest household incomes after Frogner. Ullern is repeatedly named among the districts most popular with families for exactly that reason: space, quiet and quick access to the fjord and the Bygdøy beaches. Two-bedroom rents run about NOK 22,000–28,000/month; family-sized 3-bedroom houses and flats are the more common ask here and price well above that. Commuting is easy in both directions — local trains and tram 13 to the centre in 10–15 minutes, and E18 west towards Bærum, which makes Ullern the usual choice for families whose children attend Oslo International School in Bekkestua without wanting to leave the city.
rows.price_range_text: NOK 22,000–28,000/month for a 2BR; family houses materially higher

extras.research_note: Investropa (early 2026): 'The three Oslo neighborhoods most popular with families are Nordstrand, Ullern, and Østensjø'; premium-district 2BR band NOK 22,000–28,000.

rows.title: Nordstrand & Østensjø
rows.summary: Southern and eastern family suburbs inside the city limits — the best space-per-krone in Oslo proper.
rows.body: Nordstrand runs along the ridge above the eastern fjord shore; Østensjø sits inland around the Østensjøvannet lake and nature reserve. Both are house-and-garden Oslo: quiet streets, sports clubs, kindergartens and municipal schools, with the fjord swimming spots at Hvervenbukta and Ingierstrand a short cycle away. They are the two districts most consistently named as family favourites alongside Ullern, and rents are materially lower than the west side — a 2-bedroom typically NOK 16,000–20,000/month, with 2–3 bedroom family units in the NOK 22,000–30,000 band. The T-bane (lines 3 and 4) or the local train reaches the centre in 15–25 minutes. The main trade-off for an international household is distance from the English- and French-language schools, all of which sit west or north-west of the centre.
rows.price_range_text: NOK 16,000–20,000/month for a 2BR; NOK 22,000–30,000 for 2–3BR family units

extras.research_note: Investropa (early 2026): mid-range areas 'Bjerke, Alna, Nordstrand' at NOK 16,000–20,000 for a 2BR; family 2–3BR rents NOK 22,000–30,000.

rows.title: Bærum: Bekkestua, Stabekk & Sandvika
rows.summary: The international-school suburb west of Oslo — the default choice for corporate families with children.
rows.body: Bærum is the affluent municipality immediately west of Oslo and the standard recommendation for relocating families with school-age children, because Oslo International School sits at Gamle Ringeriksvei 53 in Bekkestua. Bekkestua and Stabekk are leafy villa suburbs 15–20 minutes from central Oslo on the T-bane line 3 or the local train; Sandvika, further out, is a full town centre with a large shopping district and direct trains to Oslo S in about 12 minutes. Housing is dominated by houses and townhouses rather than flats, and asking rents for a family house commonly exceed NOK 30,000/month, though apartment rents in Sandvika are close to Oslo's mid-range bands. Bærum is also where a large share of Norway's corporate head offices sit (Lysaker, Fornebu), so many relocations here involve no Oslo commute at all.
rows.price_range_text: Family houses commonly above NOK 30,000/month; Sandvika apartments closer to NOK 18,000–24,000

extras.research_note: Investropa (early 2026): 'the western suburbs of Bærum for families with children' among the best expat reputations. OIS address per the workspace vendor directory (vendor_directory_by_city_frno.md, verified 2026-07-17) and oslointernationalschool.no.
extras.corridor_relevance: FR-NO — Oslo International School (IPC + IB DP, French B in the DP) is in Bekkestua

rows.title: Sentrum & Bjørvika (Barcode)
rows.summary: The new waterfront business core — where the corridor's tax, mobility and law firms actually sit.
rows.body: Bjørvika is the redeveloped harbour east of the central station: the Barcode row of towers along Dronning Eufemias gate, the Opera House, the Munch museum and the Deichman library. For a France→Norway or Norway→France case it is the most operationally relevant address in the city — Deloitte (Dronning Eufemias gate 14), KPMG (6A) and Vialto Partners (8) all sit on the same street, so the tax, payroll and immigration meetings a mover needs happen within a few hundred metres of each other. Living here is new-build apartment living: efficient, well insulated, no gardens, and priced at the top of the market (Bispevika is Oslo's most expensive micro-area by square metre, and 2-bedroom rents run NOK 22,000–28,000/month and above). Best for short assignments and couples who want to walk to work; families almost always trade Bjørvika for the west side or Bærum.
rows.price_range_text: NOK 22,000–28,000/month for a 2BR, premium new-build units higher

extras.research_note: Firm addresses verified 2026-08-14 from deloitte.com/no offices page, kpmg.com/no office list and vialtopartners.com/contact-us; Bispevika square-metre ranking from Investropa (early 2026).
extras.corridor_relevance: FR-NO / NO-FR — Deloitte Norway (Dronning Eufemias gate 14), KPMG Norway (6A) and Vialto Partners Oslo (8) are all on this street

rows.title: Tøyen & Gamle Oslo
rows.summary: The most affordable central option: diverse, fast-changing, 8 minutes to the centre by metro.
rows.body: Tøyen sits east of Grünerløkka around the botanical garden and the natural history museum, in the Gamle Oslo borough. It is the cheapest genuinely central part of Oslo — 1-bedrooms from about NOK 13,000/month and 2-bedrooms from the mid-NOK-teens — and the most ethnically diverse, with the Grønland market street as its commercial spine. Eight minutes to the centre on the T-bane, with the Tøyenparken green space and the Munch-era Botanical Garden as amenities. The area has gentrified quickly over the last decade and is popular with students, first-posting internationals and anyone prioritising budget and centrality over quiet. Households moving from a French metropolitan area will find the density and street life familiar; those coming with children usually look at Sagene or the west side instead.
rows.price_range_text: 1BR from about NOK 13,000/month; 2BR from the mid-NOK-teens

extras.research_note: AffordWhere Oslo dataset (official statistics compiled January 2026) lists Tøyen at '8 min metro to center, 1BR from kr13,000/mo, diverse / affordable / growing'.

rows.title: Lycée français René Cassin d'Oslo (LFO)
rows.summary: Norway's only AEFE French-curriculum school — the anchor school for the France↔Norway corridor, on two Oslo sites.
rows.body: The Lycée français René Cassin d'Oslo has taught the French national curriculum in Oslo since 1961 and is the only AEFE-accredited French school in Norway, running from maternelle through terminale (baccalauréat) for roughly 650–675 pupils from around 37 countries. It operates on TWO sites: Skovveien 9, 0257 Oslo (primary plus 6e–4e; pupil entrance at the corner of Oscars gate and Colbjørnsens gate) and Vulkan 11, 0178 Oslo (3e, 2nde, 1ère, terminale). Note the site history: the school was required to leave the Skovveien premises for a City of Oslo upgrade and added the Vulkan site — confirm which site a given year group sits on at enrolment rather than assuming a single campus. Fees are set by the René Cassin Foundation, which states its policy is to keep them at a level preserving social diversity; the published 2026/27 application fee is NOK 3,000, and French scholarship (bourse scolaire) and Lånekassen questions go to the school secretariat. The main admissions window for an August start runs 2 February – 1 March, which for a summer relocation means applying from France in the winter before the move.
rows.price_range_text: Application fee NOK 3,000 (2026/27); tuition set annually by the Fondation René Cassin — request the current schedule from the school

The Fondation page also records that the school had to leave Skovveien in spring 2025 for a municipal upgrade, so the campus split should be re-confirmed each year.

rows.title: Oslo International School (OIS)
rows.summary: English-language IB school in Bekkestua, Bærum; IPC through IB Diploma with French B available.
rows.body: Oslo International School is the long-established English-language international school for the Oslo region, located at Gamle Ringeriksvei 53 in Bekkestua, Bærum — 15–20 minutes west of central Oslo. It runs the International Primary Curriculum through to the IB Diploma Programme, with French available as a DP language B, which matters for a French pupil who needs to maintain French while switching to English-medium schooling. Admissions are rolling through the year rather than tied to a single window, which makes OIS the practical option for a move that lands mid-year. Published tuition for 2026/27 is NOK 288,700 per year — the highest of the Oslo international schools and usually only viable where an employer education allowance exists. Its Bekkestua location is the main reason relocating families choose to live in Bærum rather than central Oslo.

extras.research_note: Address, curriculum, fee and rolling-admissions facts carried from workspace research vendor_directory_by_city_frno.md (verified 2026-07-17, marked fully verified there). Re-confirm the fee each annual cycle before quoting it to a customer.
extras.corridor_relevance: FR-NO — English-medium alternative to LFO with French as a DP language B; rolling admissions suit mid-year corridor moves

rows.title: Norlights International School (NLIS)
rows.summary: Full IB continuum in Skådalen at a fraction of OIS fees — the value option, with a hard 1 March deadline.
rows.body: Norlights International School sits at Skådalsveien 33 in the Skådalen / Vinderen area of western Oslo and offers the full IB continuum in English. It is by far the most affordable of the city's international schools because it is a state-subsidised private school: published fees are NOK 43,450 per year for grades 1–10 and NOK 29,700 per year for the IB Diploma Programme — roughly a seventh of the OIS rate. The catch is timing: the application deadline for an August start is 1 March, and places in popular year groups go early, so a family whose Norwegian contract is signed in spring will often find NLIS closed for the coming year while OIS is still open. Well connected to the west-side residential districts by the Holmenkollen T-bane line, which makes Vinderen, Ullern and Frogner natural catchment areas.

extras.research_note: Address, IB continuum, fees and the 1 March deadline carried from workspace research vendor_directory_by_city_frno.md (verified 2026-07-17). Fees should be re-verified each annual cycle.
extras.corridor_relevance: FR-NO — the affordable English-medium option, but its 1 March deadline is a feasibility flag for spring-signed contracts

rows.title: Asker International School (AIS)
rows.summary: State-funded IB school in Asker, south-west of Oslo: NOK 40,500/year flat for grades 1–10, and no Diploma Programme.
rows.body: Asker International School opened in August 2013 in Asker municipality, south-west of Bærum and roughly 25–30 minutes from central Oslo by train, at Gamle Borgenvei 3, 1383 Asker. Teaching is in English under IB programmes (an IB World School since spring 2016) and the school covers grades 1–10 — there is NO Diploma Programme, so a household with a 16-plus pupil needs OIS or NLIS for the final years. Because the fees track the funding the school receives from the Department of Education, they are unusually flat and low: NOK 40,500 for calendar year 2026 for all grades, invoiced in nine instalments, plus a one-off NOK 2,000 administration fee on accepting a place; the third child is free and the fourth onwards is invoiced at 50%. AIS is the practical option for households placed along the western commuter belt (Asker, Heggedal, Slemmestad) or near the Fornebu / Lysaker / Sandvika office clusters, where an Asker address can mean no Oslo commute at all.
rows.price_range_text: NOK 40,500/year for all grades (calendar year 2026), plus a one-off NOK 2,000 administration fee; third child free, 50% from the fourth
